Well, I mean... it's hard to say exactly how other people see me, right? Because they're looking at the whole picture, the suit, the tie, the presentation, but when I look at myself, it's just... it's different. Like, okay, take this morning for example. Before I came here, I had this big meeting with a prospective client, right? And I'm standing in front of the mirror in my bathroom—it's this big, well-lit mirror, maybe almost too well-lit, honestly, because it just highlights everything. And I'm getting ready, adjusting my tie, making sure everything is perfect, but I just can't stop staring at my stomach. 

It's like my eyes just immediately zero in on my midsection, and then my face, right around the jawline. And I'll stand there, sometimes for five, ten minutes, just turning side to side, checking the profile, checking how the shirt lays flat against my stomach. And if I see even the slightest hint of... I don't know, softness? Like if the fabric doesn't fall perfectly straight, or if my face looks even a tiny bit puffy from, I don't know, maybe having too much sodium the night before... I just spiral. 

Because in my head, if I look soft, if I look like I've let myself go even a fraction of an inch, I just know they're going to see me as sloppy. Or weak. And in sales, especially wholesale manufacturing where the margins are tight and these guys are tough negotiators, if they sense weakness, they will eat you alive. They won't respect you. They'll think, "Oh, this guy can't even keep himself in check, how is he going to manage our supply chain?" So, yeah, I guess my sister and HR see this guy who's lost a lot of weight, but when I look in the mirror, all I see are these areas that still need so much work. I just see the potential to look weak, and I have to fix it before anyone else notices. So I don't know if that means I see myself differently than they do, but I definitely don't see what they're seeing when they tell me I'm too thin. I just see the flaws that I need to tighten up.

Well, I mean... "avoid" might be a strong word, but... okay, yes, I guess I do have to navigate those situations pretty carefully now. It’s just that it gets incredibly complicated. 

Like I was saying before, I am still completely managing my sales route. During the day, it's easy. I'm driving from warehouse to warehouse, I'm in control of my schedule, I can grab a black coffee and just keep moving. I'm totally fine. But the evenings... the evenings are where it becomes a real issue. In my industry, there's this whole ingrained culture of wining and dining the clients, right? You're supposed to take these guys out to these massive, old-school steakhouses to close a deal. And they want the huge ribeye, they want the loaded baked potatoes, the drinks, the heavy appetizers dripping in oil and butter. 

And I just... I can't do it. I sit there and all I can think about is how much damage that one meal is going to do to my body. If I can't look at the menu beforehand and know exactly—and I mean *exactly*—what my options are, I start to panic. I need to know I can get something completely plain, like a dry salad or steamed vegetables, where I can control what's going into it. Because if I eat what they're eating, it's just going to ruin all the progress I've made. It's going to make me look soft again. 

So, what I've started doing is, if I can't pick the restaurant myself and control the menu, I just make an excuse. I'll tell them I have a late flight to catch, or I have to prep for a morning presentation, or I'm fighting off a bug. I’ve been turning down a lot of client dinner invitations lately. 

And it's not just work, either. It's completely spilled over into my personal life. After the divorce, my buddies were trying to set me up, trying to get me back out there on dates. But dating revolves entirely around food or drinks! "Let's grab dinner," "let's get a drink." It's an absolute minefield. How do you sit across from someone you just met on a first date and explain why you're only drinking ice water and interrogating the waiter about how the chicken is cooked? You look insane. So I just... I don't go. I've been saying no to almost everything. I guess I've just been keeping to myself a lot more lately. It's just easier that way, you know? It's just fewer variables to worry about if I just stay home.

Grocery shopping? Cooking? Oh, no, no... it's actually the exact opposite. I don't avoid them at all. I mean, I *have* to do them. Significant changes? I mean... I guess it depends on what you consider a change. To me, it's just optimization. It’s the standard operating procedure now, but yeah, it is a lot different from how I used to do things when I first started in sales. 

Most days, I keep it strictly to coffee in the morning. I used to be the guy who would stop at a diner or grab a breakfast sandwich at a drive-thru while heading to my first account, but you just can't trust that stuff. It's full of grease, it slows you down, and honestly, I don't need it. The black coffee keeps me sharp. It keeps the edge. 

Then I'm out there, driving those 150, 200 miles, going from plant to plant. So between sales calls, if I really need something to just keep my focus up before a big pitch, I might have a protein bar. Just one. I keep a very specific brand in the center console of the company car—one where I know the exact macro breakdown, no hidden sugars. It's just enough fuel to get me through the afternoon without making me feel heavy or sluggish when I walk into a meeting. 

And then by the time I get home, or back to the hotel if I'm overnighting on my route, I keep it incredibly strict. I'll make something really small, like just a piece of plain grilled chicken. Absolutely no rice, no potatoes, no heavy sides. Just the lean protein. Because the thing is—and this is why the routine has to be so rigid—if I actually sit down and eat a full meal, like a normal, heavy dinner with sides and all that... it just completely ruins my headspace. It feels like I messed up the whole day. 

Like, I will literally sit there and think about how all that discipline, all that focus I maintained since my alarm went off at 4:30 AM, just got completely thrown out the window. And for what? Ten minutes of eating? It's just not worth that feeling of failure. It makes me feel sloppy, and like I said before, I cannot afford to be sloppy. So yeah, the routine is completely dialed in around that schedule. Coffee, a bar, plain chicken. It's the only way I can get through the day and still feel like I'm in control of myself.

I'd be exhausted. But I'm not. So, yeah, they might think I'm not seeing reality, but from where I'm standing, they're the ones completely ignoring the fact that I am functioning perfectly fine. It just doesn't feel like an emergency to me at all.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever avoid social situations where food is involved because you're afraid of gaining weight?\n\nPatient: Well, I mean... \"avoid\" might be a strong word, but... okay, yes, I guess I do have to navigate those situations pretty carefully now. It’s just that it gets incredibly complicated. \n\nLike I was saying before, I am still completely managing my sales route. During the day, it's easy. I'm driving from warehouse to warehouse, I'm in control of my schedule, I can grab a black coffee and just keep moving. I'm totally fine. But the evenings... the evenings are where it becomes a real issue. In my industry, there's this whole ingrained culture of wining and dining the clients, right? You're supposed to take these guys out to these massive, old-school steakhouses to close a deal. And they want the huge ribeye, they want the loaded baked potatoes, the drinks, the heavy appetizers dripping in oil and butter. \n\nAnd I just... I can't do it. I sit there and all I can think about is how much damage that one meal is going to do to my body. If I can't look at the menu beforehand and know exactly—and I mean *exactly*—what my options are, I start to panic. I need to know I can get something completely plain, like a dry salad or steamed vegetables, where I can control what's going into it. Because if I eat what they're eating, it's just going to ruin all the progress I've made. It's going to make me look soft again. \n\nSo, what I've started doing is, if I can't pick the restaurant myself and control the menu, I just make an excuse. I'll tell them I have a late flight to catch, or I have to prep for a morning presentation, or I'm fighting off a bug. I’ve been turning down a lot of client dinner invitations lately. \n\nAnd it's not just work, either. It's completely spilled over into my personal life. After the divorce, my buddies were trying to set me up, trying to get me back out there on dates. But dating revolves entirely around food or drinks! \"Let's grab dinner,\" \"let's get a drink.\" It's an absolute minefield. How do you sit across from someone you just met on a first date and explain why you're only drinking ice water and interrogating the waiter about how the chicken is cooked? You look insane. So I just... I don't go. I've been saying no to almost everything. I guess I've just been keeping to myself a lot more lately. It's just easier that way, you know? It's just fewer variables to worry about if I just stay home.\n\nDoctor: Are you avoiding any activities or events outside of work because of your concerns about weight?\n\nPatient: I mean... didn't I just... well, like I was just saying with the dating thing and my buddies, right? That's all outside of work. But if you mean, like, other specific hobbies or, I don't know, community events or something? Not really. I don't have this list of things I'm actively crossing off my calendar, if that's what you're asking. \n\nIt's more just... a general shrinking of my schedule, I guess you could say. Because, if you really think about it, what do guys my age actually do when they get together on a weekend? They don't just go for a walk in the park. They go to a sports bar to watch the game, and they order pitchers of heavy craft beer and those massive platters of nachos with the grease pooling at the bottom. Or they do a backyard barbecue where someone's grilling huge burgers and hot dogs and there's macaroni salad sitting out. I just... I can't be around that. I can't participate in that without everyone staring at me for not eating, so it's easier to just remove myself from the equation entirely. \n\nBut it's not like I'm avoiding... I don't know, going to a concert or a museum, mostly because nobody invites me to do that kind of stuff anyway, and I honestly don't have the time. Like I said, my territory is massive. My whole life right now is just managing my accounts, getting my morning miles in, and trying to keep things quiet and controlled in the evenings. So outside of the dates and the guys wanting to grab drinks or food, which I already mentioned, I can't really think of any other specific events I'm actively avoiding. I just don't really do much else anyway. My routine is pretty set, and I like it that way. It keeps things simple.\n\nDoctor: Do you think there's a difference between how you perceive your body and how it actually looks?\n\nPatient: I mean, we kind of touched on this a minute ago, right? With the whole \"reality\" thing. But if you're asking what I actually see when I look at myself... look, in my line of work, presentation is absolutely everything. You walk into a room with a regional buyer, and they make a judgment about you in the first three seconds. Before you even open your briefcase, they've decided if they respect you or not. \n\nSo, yeah, I am meticulous about how I present myself. When I'm in my hotel room getting ready, right before a big pitch meeting, or... or even back when I was trying to go on those dates I mentioned earlier, I spend a lot of time in front of the mirror. And I'm not just doing a quick glance to see if my tie is straight or if my hair is combed. I completely zero in on my stomach and my face. I will stand there under those harsh bathroom lights and just scrutinize every angle. \n\nBecause those are the telltale areas, aren't they? If I look in that mirror and I think I look even a little bit soft... it completely wrecks my headspace for the rest of the day. It’s like a physical reaction. Because I know that if I look soft, the people sitting across the table from me are going to see me as sloppy. They’re going to look at me and think I’m weak. And in wholesale sales, if they smell weakness, if they think you lack the basic discipline to keep yourself in check, why on earth would they trust you with a massive, multi-state supply contract? \n\nIt’s all connected. The discipline it takes to keep my stomach flat and my jawline sharp is the exact same discipline it takes to hit my quarterly quotas. So when HR or my family says I look \"too thin\" or whatever, that's just their skewed perspective. Because when I look in the mirror, all I'm looking for is whether I've lost my edge. If I see any softness in my cheeks, any lack of definition around my midsection, I just know I have to push harder. I can't afford to look sloppy. I just can't. So, is there a difference between how I perceive it and how it looks? I don't know. I rely on that. And then I'm in the car. I drive anywhere from, I don't know, 150 to 300 miles a day depending on which wholesale accounts I'm hitting. I'm walking into massive manufacturing plants, I'm doing inventory checks, I'm pitching to regional managers. I can't avoid any of that. That's my livelihood. If I start skipping out on my route, I lose my territory, and if I lose my territory... well, that's just not an option. Am I anxious when I'm not eating... yeah. Oh, absolutely. It's not just about the moment the food is in front of me or when I'm looking at a menu. The fear is just... it's always kind of running in the background, like this low hum, you know? It never really turns off. 

Because for me, it all comes down to the numbers. That's the ultimate judge. If I step on that scale in the morning—say it's the morning after one of those unavoidable client dinners we were talking about, or like a couple months ago when I had to go down for a weekend out in Miami with some of the regional directors—if the scale is even a pound higher, just one single pound... I get this intense panic. It just hits me right in the chest. It feels exactly like I'm completely losing control of everything. 

And the thing is, I know how the body works, right? I know logically it could be water retention from flying, or sodium from whatever restaurant they dragged me to, but that logic doesn't matter at all. The anxiety just takes over completely. Even if I'm nowhere near a kitchen, even if I'm just driving my route or sitting in a waiting room at a manufacturing plant, my brain is just spinning. I immediately start planning exactly how I'm going to cut back the next day. I'll be sitting there calculating how I can shave off calories, deciding I'm going to skip my afternoon protein bar entirely, or figuring out how I can wake up at 4:00 AM instead of 4:30 so I can add an extra three miles to my morning run. 

It's exhausting, honestly. I'll be in the middle of a pitch, talking about wholesale margins, but in the back of my head, I'm just obsessing over that one pound and how I'm going to fix it. Because if I don't fix it right then, if I don't get the control back immediately, then one pound becomes two, and then I'm sloppy. And like I said, I cannot afford to be sloppy. So, yeah, the anxiety doesn't need food to be triggered. It's just always there, waiting for me to make a mistake.

I mean... I guess if you're asking about other parts of my day, like the actual decisions I make... getting dressed in the morning is a whole ordeal now. A really, really big ordeal. 

Like, before I head out for a client meeting, or, you know, on the very rare occasion I actually try to go on a date these days, the mirror is just... it's a huge hurdle. I'll stand there, whether it's in my apartment or some random hotel bathroom with that awful fluorescent lighting on the road, and I just get completely stuck. Yeah, I mean... it goes exactly back to what I was telling you a few minutes ago about getting dressed in the morning. It's completely connected to who I am as a person. Like, when I'm standing in front of that mirror before a big pitch or... well, a date, if I ever actually went on one... and I'm zeroing in so hard on my stomach and my face. I start projecting, thinking they can see right through me, like they're looking at someone who lacks basic self-control and discipline. 

So, yeah, I can't really separate my weight from my character anymore. I just can't. They're completely tied together in my head. If I'm sharp and lean, I'm a good, successful person. If I'm soft, I'm a failure. There's really no in-between for me.

Even if I'm nowhere near a kitchen, even if I'm just driving my route or sitting in a waiting room at a manufacturing plant, my brain is just spinning. I immediately start planning exactly how I'm going to cut back the next day. I'll be sitting there calculating how I can shave off calories, deciding I'm going to skip my afternoon protein bar entirely, or figuring out how I can wake up at 4:00 AM instead of 4:30 so I can add an extra three miles to my morning run. \n\nIt's exhausting, honestly. I'll be in the middle of a pitch, talking about wholesale margins, but in the back of my head, I'm just obsessing over that one pound and how I'm going to fix it. So, yeah, the anxiety doesn't need food to be triggered. It's just always there, waiting for me to make a mistake.\n\nDoctor: Are there any parts of your daily routine, outside of eating or social events, where you feel like your fear of gaining weight is holding you back?\n\nPatient: Holding me back? I zero in entirely on my stomach and my face. It's like I get tunnel vision, you know?
